title: Incomplete synaptic vesicle priming functionally disconnects CA1 pyramidal cells
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: The hippocampal CA1 area is perceived as a nonrecurrent neuronal network, i.e., CA1 pyramidal cells (CA1PCs) within the CA1 area innervate mainly γ-aminobutyric acid–releasing interneurons but not each other. Here, we performed an unbiased examination of the functional properties of local CA1PC output synapses using in vitro two-photon glutamate imaging. Fluorescent transients measured with iGluSnFR3 in individual boutons displayed extraordinary heterogeneity in their amplitudes and short-term plasticity patterns upon a complex train of presynaptic action potential firing. Post hoc electron microscopy of the imaged boutons demonstrated that distinct postsynaptic structure-innervating boutons display different functional properties. Approximately 25% of the boutons innervate CA1PC spines, which either release glutamate with very low release probability or completely fail to release. Phorbol 12,13-dibutyrate and elevated calcium (2+) concentration, manipulations that enhance synaptic vesicle priming and fusion, convert these silent into properly functioning synapses. Our results provide evidence that CA1PCs are interconnected with structurally and molecularly intact glutamatergic synapses, but incomplete synaptic vesicle (SV) priming precludes SV release.

title: Tracing Neanderthal ancestry patterns through successive population expansions in Europe
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: During their expansion from Africa, modern humans interbred with Neanderthals, resulting in introgression of Neanderthal DNA into their genomes. This process contributed to a Southeast-to-Northwest gradient of Neanderthal ancestry across Europe. We investigate the population dynamics underlying the emergence and persistence of this gradient through two successive human range expansions. We developed a three-population, layered, spatially explicit simulation framework to track the spatiotemporal evolution of Neanderthal ancestry under a model of interactions among Neanderthals, pre-Neolithic hunter-gatherers, and Neolithic farmers. Our results indicate that the ancestry cline emerged from the interplay between the direction of the initial hunter-gatherer expansion, the northern limit of the Neanderthal range, and strong reproductive isolation, without requiring natural selection. The similar direction of the subsequent Neolithic expansion explains the cline’s persistence and Neanderthal ancestry differences between hunter-gatherers and farmers. These findings demonstrate how spatiotemporal patterns in ancient DNA provide insights into past population dynamics.

title: The ZmJAZ14–ZmMYC2 module regulates anthesis–silking synchrony in maize
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract:
The evolution of traits can increase yield potential but may create physiological constraints. Jasmonic acid (JA) signaling regulates sex determination in male (tassel) and female (ear) inflorescences in maize. Although the formation of ears laid the foundation for high yields, the asynchronous development of the tassel and the ear prolongs the anthesis-silking interval (ASI), threatening reproductive success and reducing yield. Whether JA signaling coordinates ear and tassel development remains unclear. Here, we show that the core JA signaling module, ZmJAZ14-ZmMYC2a/b, orchestrates the expression of
                    SPL29
                    for reproductive transition,
                    BA1
                    for female inflorescence initiation, and
                    EXPA5
                    for silk elongation. Coordination of these physiological processes underpins synchronous growth of the tassel and ears, whereas disruption of
                    ZmMYC2a/b
                    or accumulation of the repressor ZmJAZ14 prolongs ASI. Our work suggests that the repurposing of JA signaling to coordinate ear and tassel development may represent a lineage-specific evolutionary burden in maize. Deciphering the link between gains and unforeseen costs of evolution could further improve yields.

title: Brown carbon in biomass burning aerosol enhances HONO production
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract:
Nitrous acid (HONO) is an important source of hydroxyl radicals (•OH). •OH drives ozone and aerosol formation, affecting air quality, health, and climate. Elevated HONO concentrations have been observed in biomass burning (BB) plumes. However, the mechanism remains unclear, hindering parameterization and quantification of the impacts. Here, we conducted flow tube experiments with BB aerosol samples and proxies to investigate renoxification, a process that converts nitrate into HONO and NO
                    
                      x
                    
                    (NO and NO
                    2
                    ). Our results reveal that renoxification in BB aerosol is enhanced by brown carbon (BrC) through electron transfer to nitrate as an alternative to surface-enhanced nitrate photolysis. We develop parameterization to assess the potential global impacts of BrC-enhanced renoxification, which suggests that BrC enhances surface-level HONO production by up to one order of magnitude in BB-affected regions, with surface HONO production exceeding 1 part per trillion per hour in regions with high aerosol nitrate. These impacts are expected to worsen as BB intensifies in a warming climate.

title: Electronic hair: Transforming hair into a scalable bioelectronic interface
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: In electroencephalography, hair remains a major barrier to electrode-skin contact, limiting signal quality. Here, we introduce electronic hair (eHAIR), a strategy that converts hair into a bioelectronic interface using mixed ionic-electronic conductive polymer dyes. Hair, a keratinized filament anchored within the skin, provides a stable and naturally distributed platform for interfacing. Two complementary approaches based on polythiophene derivatives enable rapid, washable functionalization of hair bundles or semipermanent coating of individual strands. The resulting eHAIR forms conformal, low-impedance interfaces that support electrophysiological recordings with increased signal amplitude and spectral power while preserving the underlying neural dynamics without gels or rigid hardware. Beyond passive sensing, eHAIR-based organic electrochemical transistors enable local signal amplification, with gain defined by hair geometry. By repurposing hair as an active bioelectronic interface, eHAIR establishes a wearable and biointegrated platform that can be implemented from individual hairs to larger hair-covered regions.

title: Mechanical forces enable human stem cell modeling of protein aggregation cardiomyopathy
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract:
Inherited cardiomyopathies are the leading cause of heart failure in young adults, with limited therapeutic options. Desmin-related cardiomyopathy (DRM), caused by mutations to cytoskeletal proteins and their chaperones, exemplifies this challenge: Here, protein quality control is compromised, leading to toxic protein aggregates that destroy cardiomyocyte contractile machinery. One of the deadliest DRM mutations in the chaperone protein αB crystallin (CRYAB-R120G) lacks a genetically matched preclinical model: Mouse models require massive overexpression of mutant CRYAB, raising questions about physiological relevance. Here, we establish a human model of
                    CRYAB
                    -linked DRM, using induced pluripotent stem cells expressing CRYAB-R120G at near-endogenous levels. We show that three-dimensional mechanical loading, but not fatty acid–based metabolic maturation media, is essential for expressing Desmin, whose aggregation defines DRM. Using microengineered heart tissues, we found that contractile deficits are associated with impaired calcium handling, pointing to electromechanical uncoupling in DRM. Treatment with the Janus kinase 1 inhibitor itacitinib partially rescued contractility, providing a functional validation of this emerging therapeutic strategy.

title: A fully hydrogel implantable patch for in situ ultrasonic monitoring of gastric leakage
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: Gastric leakage is a common and life-threatening postoperative complication, while delayed detection often leads to severe abdominal organ damage. Current radiological imaging modalities are limited in their ability to provide timely detection of gastric leakage, while the mechanical mismatch and long-term persistence of conventional electronic sensors limit their implantable applications. In this work, we developed a fully hydrogel-based ultrasonic metagel patch (USMP) for direct, real-time monitoring of gastric leakage via ultrasound imaging. The USMP incorporates a tree-ring air cell array, in which densely distributed air cells arranged in concentric rings create a strong back-scattering effect, thereby producing distinctive and stable ultrasound imaging signatures for rapid and sensitive detection. The air cells are encapsulated within biocompatible, hydrolytically degradable pH-responsive hydrogels, forming a fully hydrogel sensing architecture. The potential of the USMP for gastric leakage monitoring up to 7 days postimplantation is validated in the live rabbit model.

title: Weak adsorption, strong consequences: How trace gases control ice growth and quasi-liquid-layer structure
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: Gases in the atmosphere are often treated as passive background species in cold environments, yet their molecular roles at icy interfaces remain poorly understood. Here, we show how hydrophobic and hydrophilic trace gases can actively reorganize the ice interface and regulate freezing through interfacial stabilization. We find these gases can actively modulate both the kinetics and thermodynamics of the water-ice interface. Using molecular simulations, we find that all gases examined retard ice-front propagation relative to pure water to different extents. This slowing arises from weak but preferential adsorption at the water-ice interface, where gases occupy water-dense interfacial layers and locally suppress ice-like ordering. After freezing is complete, gases do not distribute uniformly across the frozen surface, but partition selectively among multiple adsorption regions across the ice–quasi-liquid-layer (QLL)–air interfacial landscape. Relatively hydrophobic gases exhibit a three-region adsorption pattern, whereas relatively hydrophilic gases occupy only two dominant adsorption regions. Despite these differences, both classes preferentially accumulate near the QLL-air boundary and its immediate outer region rather than the ice-QLL interface. There, gases pair with and compensate for dangling surface bonds (through a surface-passivating effect reminiscent of ligand stabilization), reducing the thermodynamic driving force for premelting and thereby thinning the QLL. These results establish a unified molecular picture in which atmospheric gases are active interfacial modulators of both ice growth and ice structure, with implications for freezing, ice-cloud microphysics, and heterogeneous atmospheric chemistry.

title: Structural insights into light harvesting and photosystem II evolution in the basal streptophyte Mesostigma viride
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract:
The basal streptophyte
                    Mesostigma viride
                    represents a critical evolutionary transition toward land plants, yet the molecular basis of its ancestral light-harvesting strategy remains elusive. Here, we present a 2.25-angstrom resolution cryo-EM structure of the
                    M. viride
                    PSII-LHCII-LHCP supercomplex, revealing a unique C
                    2
                    S
                    2
                    M
                    p2
                    L
                    p2
                    -type architecture. Our structure reveals a nearly complete set of conserved PSII core subunits, indicating that much of the PSII structural framework found in terrestrial plants was established early in the streptophyte lineage. At the periphery, the complex features a specialized antenna module in which two ancestral LHCP monomers flank CP29. These ancestral antenna proteins bind an unusually high number of carotenoids, with seven carotenoids per subunit, and extensively incorporate marine-type keto carotenoids, siphonaxanthin, and siphonein, throughout the complex, thereby broadening absorption in the blue-green region. The canonical LHCII trimer exhibits a distinctive chlorophyll
                    b
                    macrocluster and a 96-femtosecond ultrafast energy transfer component. Together, these findings provide a high-resolution molecular framework for an evolutionary intermediate that combines high-capacity aquatic light harvesting with structural features potentially relevant to photoprotection during the transition toward terrestrial life.

title: Inhibition of aberrant astrocyte activity restores auditory sensorimotor function in zebrafish spen mutants
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract:
Sensorimotor deficits can profoundly affect the life quality of patients with neurological disorders, yet our understanding of central dysfunction at the cellular or circuit level is limited. Using a forward genetic approach to generate loss of auditory function in zebrafish larvae, we identified a recessive mutation in
                    split ends
                    (
                    spen
                    ), which encodes a transcription factor implicated in neurodevelopmental disorders in humans. We found that auditory sensorimotor deficits in
                    spen
                    mutants are associated with chronically elevated calcium levels in hindbrain radial astrocytes. Astrocytes have been previously implicated in the integration of neuronal inputs that alter arousal states and sensorimotor behavior. Inhibition of noradrenergic receptors, which are expressed in astrocytes, lowered calcium levels in mutant radial astrocytes and, notably, restored behavioral responses to sound in
                    spen
                    mutants. Our study highlights a role for noradrenergic signaling in
                    spen
                    -related disease and points to potential therapeutic approaches for pediatric patients.

title: Piezoelectrically actuated magnetic dipole twisting resonators enable miniaturized low-frequency antennas
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: Miniaturized low-frequency antennas are essential for underwater, underground, and biomedical communications, yet their performance is constrained by the fundamental size-efficiency trade-off, a long-standing physical bottleneck. Here, we introduce a radiation mechanism that circumvents this constraint by replacing the time-varying currents in conventional antennas with the mechanical twisting oscillation of a magnetic dipole. Using piezoelectrically actuated, biomimetic twisting resonators with ultrahigh mechanical quality factors, we demonstrate that low-frequency antennas operating at 15.4 and 668 hertz can be miniaturized to centimeter- and millimeter-scale, respectively, with radiation efficiencies exceeding those of size-matched loop antennas by factors of 49,000 and 5000, respectively. This electromechanical-magnetic transduction enables underwater cross-medium communication over 115 meters with only milliwatt-level power consumption, using 99.9% less power than loop antennas. It also supports implantable wireless devices that achieve a fourfold increase in communication range at identical power consumption, opening a route to long-range, low-power wireless systems capable of operating in some of the most demanding environments.

title: Cell adhesion molecule–related proteins signal to promote cytoneme elongation from Sonic Hedgehog–producing cells
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: Tissue morphogenesis and postdevelopmental homeostasis rely on efficient information exchange between communicating cells. Cytonemes are actin-based protrusions that contribute to precise information flow by facilitating contact-mediated directional transport of diverse signaling cargoes. How pathway-specific cytonemes are formed is poorly understood, as are the molecular mechanisms promoting actin organization for elongation and stability of the dynamic cellular extensions. We investigated biogenesis of Sonic Hedgehog (SHH) cytonemes, revealing functional repurposing of cell adhesion molecule-related proteins Brother of CDON (BOC) and Cell adhesion molecule-related, Down-regulated by Oncogenes (CDON) into recruiters of actin regulators FARP1 and Cdc42 for cytoneme elongation. Loss of BOC and CDON function blunts protrusion-localized Cdc42 activity, reducing cytoneme lengths and occurrence in SHH-expressing cells. Live imaging of developing murine spinal cords reveals that CDON loss in SHH-expressing cells reduces the frequency of neuroepithelial cytonemes and alters neuronal cell fate specification. These results inform a model whereby SHH-binding proteins promote ligand transport through stimulating formation of long cytonemes.

title: Basin-scale changes in net primary production from the biogeochemical-Argo array
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: Marine net primary production is expected to be affected by climate change. Although remote sensing offers broad spatial and temporal coverage, it is limited to surface observations and cannot capture subsurface variability. Autonomous profiling floats provide critical depth-resolved measurements that help bridge this gap. Here, we use data from the biogeochemical-Argo array to estimate basin-scale change in net primary production using the carbon-based production algorithm. We find statistically significant negative trends across the Atlantic and Southern Oceans and positive trends in the Pacific Ocean. These changes, if occurring in response to climate forcing, raise concern due to the key role of phytoplankton productivity in sustaining marine ecosystems. These trends typically agree in direction and magnitude with those from satellites. Our findings highlight the value of the biogeochemical-Argo array in detecting change in ocean productivity, demonstrating its potential for sustained monitoring. These results underscore the need for integrated observing systems to capture the full extent of changing marine productivity.

title: Does government-assisted relocation help households
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: Climate change is intensifying floods and storms, leading governments to consider relocating households away from high-risk areas. Yet, there is little evidence on whether such programs reduce risk or improve household well-being. I evaluate the US Federal Emergency Management Agency’s property acquisition (“buyout”) program using nationwide longitudinal records that track households before and after approval. By comparing households facing similar mapped flood risks, I estimate the program’s effects on relocation, residence in high-risk flood areas, and financial outcomes. Households that participate are more likely to relocate outside Federal Emergency Management Agency–designated flood hazard areas and experience short-term reductions in debt and improvements in neighborhood socioeconomic conditions. However, these benefits are concentrated among participants from wealthier and predominantly white neighborhoods, who relocate more quickly and achieve larger reductions in risk. A benefit-cost analysis shows that the program value depends on implementation costs and realized reductions in flood-risk exposure, with benefit-cost ratios ranging from 0.84 to 1.28 across three scenarios. These results show that government-assisted relocation can be an effective adaptation tool, but its social and economic benefits remain unevenly distributed.

title: Phototropin-mediated blue light signaling orients the asymmetry of Marchantia polymorpha spores
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract:
Multicellular organisms produced by sexual reproduction develop from single cells, and the asymmetry of these cells can define the orientation of the earliest developmental axes. The haploid multicellular stage of the plant,
                    Marchantia polymorpha,
                    develops from a single cell—the spore—that divides asymmetrically, producing an apical germ cell that generates the plant body and a smaller basal cell that differentiates as an anchoring germ rhizoid cell. We show that the orientation of this asymmetric cell division is controlled by an external environmental cue—blue light—that is perceived by the photoreceptor phototropin. This process requires the NCH1 (NRL PROTEIN FOR CHLOROPLAST MOVEMENT 1) protein for downstream signaling. Together, these findings define core elements of the mechanism by which a directional environmental signal orients cell division, which, in turn, orients the first axis of symmetry.

title: Nonlinear cooling and control of a mechanical quantum harmonic oscillator
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: Nonlinearities are a key feature allowing nonclassical control of quantum harmonic oscillators. However, when nonlinearities are strong, designing protocols for control is often difficult, placing a barrier to exploiting these properties fully. In this work, using a single trapped-ion oscillator operated in the strongly nonlinear regime of the atom-light interaction, we show how to generate localized multi (two, three, four, and five)–component Schrödinger’s cat manifolds using a novel form of nonlinear reservoir engineering. We then specifically select Hamiltonians which allow us to perform measurements on these state manifolds. Our work demonstrates the experimental use of high-order nonlinear processes for control of nonclassical states of a quantum harmonic oscillator, opening up a new toolbox which can be applied to bosonic quantum error correction, computation, and sensing.

title: Input-specific deployment of the active zone scaffold RIM tunes synaptic release probability and plasticity
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract:
The multidomain scaffold RIM (Rab3-interacting molecule) is widely viewed as a broadly required organizer of the presynaptic active zone, clustering voltage-gated Ca
                    2+
                    (Ca
                    v
                    2) channels, priming synaptic vesicles, and supporting neurotransmitter release. Whether this reliance is uniform across synapses with distinct release probabilities, however, has been difficult to resolve at convergent inputs. Here, using neurotoxin-based silencing to isolate transmission at the
                    Drosophila
                    neuromuscular junction, we show that the requirement for RIM is highly input-specific: RIM is essential to empower transmission at a high–release probability phasic synapse, yet is largely dispensable at a neighboring low–release probability tonic synapse. This specificity extends to plasticity: RIM is required for acute homeostatic potentiation at the phasic input, but not for chronic potentiation at the tonic input. Super-resolution imaging reveals that RIM is positioned closer to Ca
                    v
                    2 channels at phasic synapses and, during acute plasticity, coordinates their nanoscale reorganization to drive the rapid expansion of the readily releasable pool.

title: A LiDAR-based reconstruction reveals increasing Arctic phytoplankton production during low-light winter-shoulder period
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract:
Arctic marine productivity is traditionally considered concentrated in the sunlit season, yet low-light winter-shoulder periods remain poorly constrained because passive ocean color observations require sufficient solar illumination. Here, we use 2.39 million spaceborne LiDAR profiles from CALIOP (2006–2023) to reconstruct Arctic net primary production (NPP) and evaluate how active-sensor observations reduce this seasonal blind spot. The bio-optical retrieval model was trained using MODIS-constrained observations under illuminated conditions; accordingly, low-light estimates represent physically constrained extrapolations beyond the primary MODIS-observable training domain rather than direct NPP measurements. Within this framework, LiDAR increases winter half-year observational coverage from ∼20 to 30% to ∼70 to 75% and reveals widespread low-light winter-shoulder production across marginal seas and seasonal ice-edge regions. Pan-Arctic NPP integrated over this period increased at an estimated rate of 0.75 Tg C year
                    −1
                    during 2007–2023, whereas the corresponding passive-sensor signal was negligible. Accounting for this component raises annual Arctic NPP estimates by ∼13.3% indicating that passive sensor-based assessments may underrepresent the magnitude and seasonal structure of Arctic productivity. Associations with declining sea ice and surface warming suggest this underrepresented production is consistent with ongoing seasonal reorganization of Arctic carbon fixation. Uncertainties from model parameterization, low-light extrapolation, and limited in situ validation are largest in the lowest-light and highest-latitude regimes. These findings do not imply photosynthesis during absolute polar night, but show that active LiDAR observations with explicit light constraints and transparent extrapolation limits can test how unresolved low-light winter-shoulder production may alter Arctic NPP seasonality under continuing sea-ice loss.

title: A TROP2-targeting aptamer enables selective drug delivery and potent antitumor activity in pancreatic cancer
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract:
Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) remains difficult to treat, highlighting the need for strategies that selectively deliver cytotoxic agents to tumor cells. Trophoblast cell-surface antigen 2 (TROP2) has been proposed as a candidate therapeutic target in PDAC, but non-antibody-based delivery formats remain underexplored. Using protein-SELEX, we identified T17, a high-affinity aptamer that specifically binds to TROP2, and conjugated it to monomethyl auristatin E through an MC-Val-Cit-PAB linker to generate the aptamer-drug conjugate T17-M. Preclinical evaluation in cellular and animal models showed that T17-M retained TROP2-dependent binding, underwent clathrin-mediated internalization and lysosomal processing, and suppressed tumor growth in cell-line-derived and patient-derived xenografts. T17-M also reduced liver metastasis and induced calreticulin exposure, ATP release, and HMGB1 secretion, consistent with immunogenic cell death. In immunocompetent models, T17-M promoted dendritic-cell activation and CD8
                    +
                    T cell infiltration, while its combination with PD-1 blockade further enhanced tumor control and prolonged survival. These findings provide preclinical proof-of-concept for T17-M as an alternative TROP2-targeted drug-delivery strategy for PDAC.

title: Phosphatases regulating ERK activation and ERK-dependent cell migration
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract:
Extracellular signal-regulated kinases (ERKs) have essential roles in development and are implicated in numerous diseases. ERKs are activated by phosphorylation and are regulated by dephosphorylation. To study the ERK phosphatases, we adapted a method to monitor ERK activity in live, unfixed preparations that accommodates the highly dynamic temporal and spatial features of ERK activation. We evaluated 140 human phosphatases using an in vivo reporter (ERK-SPARK) for high-throughput screening in human cells, and we used an in vivo
                    Drosophila
                    model for functional validation of their phosphatase homologs. We found that EYA family phosphatases are critical regulators of ERK signaling both in
                    Drosophila
                    and in mammalian cells and found that inhibition of human EYA4, a homolog of
                    Drosophila
                    Eyes Absent phosphatase, enhances migration of ERK-responsive tumor cells. These findings have important implications for the development of therapeutics.

title: Cocrystals for sequestering and separating large PAHs
source: AAAS: Science Advances: Table of Contents
abstract: Highly adaptive boroxine organic assemblies (BOAs) derived from a boronic acid and a linear alkene function as a first-generation constitutional dynamic library (CDL) to sequester and separate large polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) in form of cocrystals. Configurational and conformational isomerism of the organoboroxines in host-guest assemblies is induced by electronic properties, shape and size of the PAHs through a “shrink-wrap” process/mechanism, which reveals a templating role of the PAH during the CDL assembly. The CDL was applied to separate up to three different PAHs. The cocrystals exhibit tunable electronic properties. The CDL afforded a cocrystal wherein alkenes of two different BOAs undergo [2 + 2] photocycloaddition in the same solid.

title: Chromatin dynamics secondary to dexamethasone exposure identifies 67 genes linked to elevated IOP and primary open-angle glaucoma
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract: Primary open-angle glaucoma (POAG) is a chronic neurodegenerative disorder, and elevated intraocular pressure (IOP) represents its only modifiable risk factor. We modeled increased IOP by treating three primary human trabecular meshwork cell strains with dexamethasone and generated a high-resolution map of promoter-centered chromatin contacts and regulatory modules. We identify dynamic changes in chromatin compartments and looping, cis-regulatory elements, and transcription factor hubs corresponding to altered expression profile. By integrating Genomewide association studies associated variants with dexamethasone induced chromatin landscape, we ascertain 29 target genes linked to 23 lead IOP variants and 57 genes for 46 POAG variants, with 19 shared between the two. Pathway analysis of 67 IOP- and POAG-associated genes reveals enrichment in vesicle transport, TLR, MAPK, and hippo-YAP signaling pathways. We also uncover transcriptional regulatory role of 103 noncoding lead variants. Our studies provide a mechanistic framework of genetic complexity accompanying steroid-induced IOP and related POAG pathology.

title: PPP1R1B differentially modulates alcohol intake and emotional comorbidity through distinct prefrontal circuits
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract: Excessive alcohol consumption frequently co-occurs with anxiety and depression in alcohol use disorder (AUD), yet the specific neural circuits and molecular mechanisms coordinating these comorbid conditions remain poorly defined. The medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC), particularly its prelimbic (PL) and infralimbic (IL) subregions, projects to key reward and emotion centers like the nucleus accumbens (Nac) and basolateral amygdala (BLA), but the functional heterogeneity of these projections is unclear. Using chemogenetics, retrograde tracing, electrophysiology, spatial proteomics, and cell-type-specific gene editing in mice subjected to a 4-wk intermittent access to alcohol (IAA) paradigm, we selectively manipulated glutamatergic projections from the PL and IL to the Nac core, Nac shell, and BLA and assessed alcohol intake, anxiety-like, and depression-like behaviors. Chemogenetic activation of PL-Nac core projections reduced short-term alcohol intake, anxiety-, and depression-like behaviors, while IL-BLA activation decreased alcohol consumption and anxiety-like behaviors only. Retrograde tracing revealed mirror-image anatomical segregation of projection-defined neuronal subpopulations within PL/IL linking spatial organization to functional divergence. IAA induced pathway-specific synaptic adaptations. Spatial proteomics nominated protein phosphatase 1 regulatory subunit 1B (PPP1R1B) as a candidate molecule in PL-Nac core neurons. Independent immunostaining confirmed PPP1R1B downregulation, and circuit-specific knockout recapitulated alcohol-related and affective phenotypes, whereas overexpression reversed them. In IL-BLA neurons, PPP1R1B manipulation modulated alcohol intake and anxiety, but not depression. These findings define a subregion- and projection-specific organizational logic in the mPFC for differentially regulating alcohol consumption and emotional comorbidity, with PPP1R1B as a key molecular determinant. This provides a neural pathway–molecule framework for targeted intervention in AUD.

title: Multi-omics characterization of white matter free water reveals genetic and vascular determinants of neurological disorders
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract: White matter free water (FW-WM), quantified using diffusion MRI, reflects extracellular water content and microstructural alterations within water matter, but its genetic architecture and clinical relevance remain largely uncharted. We conducted a multi-omics study integrating 42,039 individuals from the UK Biobank and Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative cohorts to characterize tract-specific FW-WM across genetic, phenotypic, and proteomic dimensions. Genome-wide association analyses identified 27 independent loci and prioritized 88 genes, which were enriched in the genomic functional elements of vascular endothelial cells, pericytes, and astrocytes. Notably, 20 loci (74%) were novel compared to conventional white matter metrics. Both genetic predisposition to higher FW-WM and imaging-derived FW-WM were associated with a spectrum of neurological disorders. Specifically, imaging-derived FW-WM showed strong associations with stroke (OR = 3.14) and dementia (OR = 4.15), while higher baseline FW-WM predicted progression from MCI to AD (HR = 2.58). Bidirectional Mendelian randomization analyses further supported genetically predicted associations between hypertension and FW-WM, which were together associated with increased risks of stroke and cognitive impairment. Integrative proteomic analyses further nominated PEAR1 and ANGL3 as candidate proteins potentially linking hypertension-related vascular processes to FW-WM variation. Together, these findings provide a multi-omics characterization of FW-WM that connects genetic susceptibility, vascular factors, and neurological outcomes, supporting FW-WM as a tract-specific imaging phenotype with potential utility for neurological risk stratification.

title: Recurrent hybridization between highly divergent paramecium species
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract:
The process of speciation, through which two reproductively isolated species emerge from an ancestral population, is often gradual, including a period during which gene flow still occurs, and hence speciation remains reversible. However, if isolation persists, the progressive accumulation of genetic incompatibilities ultimately locks the speciation process, reaching the point where hybrid offspring are inviable or sterile. In plants and animals, the establishment of species barriers is quite rapid: Beyond a net genetic divergence of 0.02 substitutions per synonymous site, interspecific introgressions become extremely rare. Here we report that in ciliates, species barriers can be broken despite huge genetic divergence. We show that the genome of
                    Paramecium sonneborni
                    contains hundreds of DNA segments that were acquired by recurrent horizontal transfers from multiple very distant lineages (synonymous divergence ~1 substitution/site). These segments approach the size of full-length chromosomes, which indicates that they were introgressed by interspecific mating. These data show that in the ancestry of
                    P. sonneborni
                    , hybridization events with highly divergent species occurred repeatedly and led to viable and fertile offspring. We propose that this unexpected promiscuous sexual behavior is made possible by the fact that paramecia separate somatic and germline functions in two types of nuclei: The elimination of non-self-DNA fragments during the development of the somatic genome allows individuals of a species to remain phenotypically the same, despite recurrent genetic flow from distant species into their germline.

title: Dormancy stabilizes structured food webs
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract: Theory predicts that strong species interactions drive instability in large ecosystems, but strong interactions are common in nature while strong instability appears rare. This discrepancy motivates enduring interest in ecological mechanisms that limit or counteract instability. Dormancy—reversible metabolic suppression—may be one. Dormancy is a ubiquitous life history trait found in organisms ranging from bacteria to trees. Dormant individuals form “seed banks” that are temporarily disengaged from demographic processes and species interactions, creating a memory of past ecological dynamics. Seed banks can stabilize predator–prey interactions, but whether, when, and how they affect the stability of larger ecological networks is uncertain. We show that dormancy stabilizes oscillatory dynamics in a minimal mathematical model and illustrate how dormancy converts high oscillation frequency into strong restoring force. We find that dormancy can have qualitative stabilizing effects in structured food webs that undergo Hopf bifurcations and exhibit oscillatory instability, but rarely in unstructured networks or networks with symmetric (competitive or mutualistic) interactions. This classification remains accurate when only some species go dormant and drive stabilization. Our results clarify when dormancy can promote stability, indicating that it may be an important but overlooked stabilizing factor in food webs.

title: Physiologic and pharmacologic role of the glucocorticoid receptor in germinal center B cells and plasmacytic differentiation
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract:
In diffuse large B cell lymphoma (DLBCL), a malignancy derived from germinal center (GC) B cells, somatic hypermutation aberrantly targets glucocorticoid receptor (GR) binding sequences in the super-enhancer (SE) of multiple oncogenes. These events abrogate GR binding and deregulate the expression of the SE-linked gene, suggesting an important role of GR in normal and transformed GC B cells. Using a GC-specific
                    Nr3c1
                    knockout mouse model and multi-omics analyses in murine and human GC B cells, here we show that, under physiological conditions, GR constitutively localizes to the nucleus, where it transcriptionally modulates signaling pathways implicated in GC homeostasis and plasmablast differentiation in part by antagonizing the repressive function of BCL6 on the plasma cell master regulators IRF4 and PRDM1. While loss of baseline GR activity led to mild GC hyperplasia and impaired plasmacytic differentiation, pharmacologic doses of glucocorticoids, a key component of DLBCL chemo-immunotherapy, were preferentially toxic to GC in a GC B cell–autonomous manner. These findings uncover a physiological role for GR in the GC reaction as well as in promoting plasmablast/plasma cell formation and provide insights into the specific activity of glucocorticoids in the treatment of DLBCL.

title: Structural insights into the evolution of mitochondrial protein import from the trypanosome ATOM complex
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract:
The translocase of the outer membrane (TOM) mediates the import of most mitochondrial preproteins. In the protozoan parasite
                    Trypanosoma brucei
                    , this machinery is replaced by the atypical translocase of the outer membrane (ATOM), whose composition differs substantially from the canonical TOM complexes of fungi and metazoans. Here, we report the cryoelectron microscopy structure of the
                    T. brucei
                    ATOM complex at 2.8 Å resolution. The structure resolves all previously identified components together with an additional, previously uncharacterized subunit. Despite its divergent composition, ATOM retains a conserved dimeric channel architecture and a protein-conducting pathway closely resembling those of opisthokont TOM complexes, indicating that the core mechanism of mitochondrial protein translocation was established early in eukaryotic evolution. In contrast, the receptor and intermembrane-space regions exhibit distinct architectures, revealing extensive evolutionary diversification and multiple examples of convergent evolution. Together, these findings provide a near-atomic view of the ATOM translocase and offer insights into the origin, conservation, and diversification of the mitochondrial protein import machinery across eukaryotes.

title: Modest loss of sleep increases susceptibility to cybersecurity threats
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract: Sleep restriction leads to impaired cognitive processing across domains. I examined whether the transition to daylight saving time (DST), typically accompanied by compromised sleep, would lead to an increase in the probability of falling prey to a simulated phishing attack using a fully naturalistic experiment with random assignment and blinding. A predatory email was sent to employees at the University of California, Irvine (N = 11,218) either on the morning of Monday following the transition to DST or one week earlier. The transition led to a ~13% increase in the probability of clicking a suspicious link, without affecting the probability of opening the email or reporting it as spam. These results demonstrate that even modest, mundane, and acute loss of sleep has real-life, potentially hazardous, implications for cognitive function.

title: Wearable interstitial fluid sensing of time-resolved uric acid for early prediction of flare-associated pain in an induced mouse model
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract: Gout flare is driven by hyperuricemia (HUA) and inflammatory responses to monosodium urate (MSU) crystals, yet single time-point serum uric acid (UA) measurements cannot capture the biochemical dynamics preceding flare onset or explain the timing of severe pain manifestation. Here, we present a skin-attachable interstitial fluid (ISF)-based electrochemical sensing platform for time-resolved, minimally invasive UA monitoring in a controlled, induced mouse model of gout flare-associated inflammation and pain. The platform integrates an enzyme-based UA sensor, a thin insertion electrode, and battery-free near-field communication (NFC), enabling time-resolved in vivo tracking of ISF UA dynamics. By establishing disease-stage-specific models comprising HUA, MSU-only inflammation, and gouty arthritis flare (GA flare) conditions, we separately examined metabolic and inflammatory contributions to flare-associated UA dynamics. Time-resolved ISF monitoring revealed that the GA flare group exhibited pronounced UA fluctuation patterns that were not reproduced by either condition alone. The peak timing of UA dynamics was temporally decoupled from pain-related behavioral responses, indicating that flare-associated pain onset cannot be explained by a single UA concentration. A machine learning framework using ISF UA time-series features identified predictive information preceding peak pain, whereas analyses using earlier events defined by sustained decreases in paw withdrawal threshold showed lower and event-definition-dependent performance. These findings establish time-resolved ISF UA monitoring as a framework for resolving flare-associated biochemical dynamics and evaluating subsequent pain progression in an induced mouse model.

title: Phylogenetic profiling reveals evolutionary coupling between methyltransferases and the cytoskeleton
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract: Methylation is a fundamental post-translational modification best understood as regulating chromatin structure and gene expression, yet there is emerging evidence that methylation also shapes cytoskeletal organization, regulating key processes such as mitosis and cell migration. Proteomic studies have revealed cytoskeletal protein methylation is widespread, however little is known about the enzymes responsible for these modifications, or their evolutionary relationship to other, better known substrates for methylation, such as chromatin. To address this question, we applied phylogenetic profiling across the complete repertoire of human methyltransferases to identify conserved functional relationships extending beyond chromatin. Unbiased clustering revealed extensive coevolution between methyltransferases and many components of the cytoskeleton, uncovering a previously unrecognized evolutionary network linking canonical chromatin regulatory enzymes to cellular structural systems. Evolutionary Trace analysis of the H3K36 methyltransferase family recovered known catalytic and regulatory domains while identifying additional evolutionarily constrained residues, suggesting previously unappreciated functional interfaces. Comparative analyses further distinguished deeply conserved methyltransferase–cytoskeletal relationships from those that emerged later during eukaryotic evolution, indicating that cytoskeletal methylation comprises both ancient and lineage-expanded regulatory programs. Leveraging these evolutionary signatures, we identified and experimentally validated a previously unrecognized association between the methyltransferase NSD3 and α-tubulin. Together, these findings reveal that methyltransferases traditionally viewed as chromatin regulators participate in an evolutionarily conserved network that coordinates nuclear and cytoskeletal functions. More broadly, they establish phylogenetic profiling as a powerful approach for discovering noncanonical activities of chromatin-associated enzymes and suggest that regulation of chromatin organization and cellular architecture evolved as interconnected processes.

title: RE1 silencing transcription factor is reduced in endometriosis, and uterine deletion in mice alters progesterone responsiveness
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract:
Endometriosis is a steroid-dependent gynecologic disease characterized by progesterone (P4) resistance, subfertility/infertility, and pelvic pain; however, the molecular mechanisms underlying impaired P4 responsiveness in endometriosis tissue are not fully understood. RE1 silencing transcription factor (REST), a transcriptional regulator implicated in steroid hormone signaling, has emerged as a potential mediator of P4 responsiveness. Here, we investigated the role of REST in endometriosis using human tissues and a uterine-specific Rest conditional knockout mouse model. Immunohistochemical analysis of eutopic endometrium and ectopic lesions from patients with endometriosis revealed significantly reduced nuclear REST expression compared with control endometrium, suggesting loss of functional REST in disease. To assess the physiological consequences of REST deficiency, uterine-specific Rest knockout (Rest
                    d/d
                    ) mice were generated. Rest
                    d/d
                    females exhibited progressive subfertility and hyperestrogenic uterine tissue characteristics that displayed a blunted responsiveness to P4 treatment. Loss of Rest selectively altered expression of P4-responsive genes associated with endometriosis pathology, despite preserved P4 receptor expression. Following induction of experimental endometriosis, female mice that developed endometriotic-like lesions using Rest-deficient donor tissue developed significantly larger lesions that were less responsive to P4 treatment compared to lesions induced using control tissue. Mechanical sensitivity was modestly increased in mice receiving Rest-deficient tissue, whereas vaginal hyperalgesia was unaffected. These findings identify loss of nuclear REST as a feature of endometriosis and support a role of REST in subfertility, lesion progression, and blunted response to P4. REST may represent a molecular contributor to altered P4 responsiveness and a potential therapeutic target in endometriosis.

title: Phase transition in a dryland shrub–grass ecosystem: Emergence through local trade-offs
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract: Ecosystems are complex adaptive systems in which local interactions among individuals shape macroscopic phenomena such as pattern formation, multistability, and critical transitions. However, how such bottom-up interactions govern emergent behaviors and system-level complexity remains a central challenge in ecology. Phase transition theory, a classic paradigm in physics, links local interaction rules to emergent changes in macroscopic system states, offering a formal language for understanding cross-scale dynamics. Here we unite this theory with empirical evidence from dryland shrub–grass ecosystems and show that these systems exhibit three hallmarks of phase transitions. First, abrupt shifts separate different phases of deserts, shrublands, and grasslands. Second, shrublands and grasslands self-organize into Turing-like phase patterns, contrasting with homogeneous deserts. Third, special phenomena emerge near-transition threshold, including patch enlargement and abrupt decline at desert–vegetation interface, and fairy circles within the shrub–grass transition zone. Using a cellular automaton model built on a fundamental trade-off between extensive and intensive resource foraging strategies (EI trade-off), we show how kernels encoding local trade-offs integrate these seemingly disparate phenomena within a unified phase transition framework. Moreover, this EI trade-off was empirically validated through analyses of plant functional traits and spatial patterns of plant patches. These findings illustrate that dryland ecosystem dynamics reflect universal self-organization principles. Our work establishes phase-transition theory as a powerful framework for understanding, predicting, and managing complexity in dryland ecosystems, which advances the integration of complexity science with ecology, offering a pathway toward bottom-up ecosystem understanding.

While this tradeoff is well documented in simplified environments, its behavior in realistic three-dimensional environments remains unclear. Here, we analyze intermittent Lévy walks in three dimensions and show that search efficiency becomes strongly dependent on target geometry, with volume, surface area, and elongation governing performance across the Lévy spectrum.
